algorithms.name: Selection Sort
algorithms.definition: Selection Sort is an in-place comparison sort that divides the array into a sorted subarray and an unsorted subarray, repeatedly finding the minimum element from the unsorted subarray and moving it to the beginning.
algorithms.working_principle: In pass i (from 0 to n-2), find the index of the smallest element in arr[i...n-1]. Swap this minimum element with arr[i]. After pass i, the first i+1 elements are guaranteed to be sorted.
dry_run: Pass 0 (i=0): Scan arr[0..4]. Min is 11 at index 4. Swap arr[0] (64) with arr[4] (11) -> [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]
Pass 1 (i=1): Scan arr[1..4]. Min is 12 at index 2. Swap arr[1] (25) with arr[2] (12) -> [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]
Pass 2 (i=2): Scan arr[2..4]. Min is 22 at index 3. Swap arr[2] (25) with arr[3] (22) -> [11, 12, 22, 25, 64]
Pass 3 (i=3): Scan arr[3..4]. Min is 25 at index 3. No swap needed -> [11, 12, 22, 25, 64]
Array fully sorted in n-1 = 4 passes.

time_complexity.best: O(n^2) (Still executes (n-1)*n/2 comparisons even if array is already sorted)

algorithms.stability: Unstable (e.g. [4a, 5, 4b, 2] -> 4a gets swapped to the end behind 4b)

viva_questions.question: What is the primary advantage of selection sort?
viva_questions.answer: It makes at most O(n) swaps (at most n-1 swaps), making it valuable when writing to memory is expensive (such as Flash memory/EEPROM).

viva_questions.question: Why is selection sort O(n^2) even in the best case?
viva_questions.answer: Because the inner loop must always scan to the very end of the unsorted portion to guarantee that no smaller element exists.

algorithms.name: Bubble Sort
algorithms.definition: Bubble Sort is a comparison-based algorithm where each pair of adjacent elements is compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order. This process repeats until no swaps are needed.
algorithms.working_principle: In pass 0, the largest element 'bubbles up' to the last position arr[n-1]. In pass 1, the second largest bubbles up to arr[n-2]. An optimized version uses a 'swapped' flag to terminate early in O(n) time if the array is already sorted.
dry_run: Pass 2: (1>2 no) -> (2>4 no) -> No swaps occurred! Early termination triggered.

time_complexity.best: O(n) (When array is already sorted, detected by swapped flag in 1 pass)
time_complexity.worst: O(n^2) (When array is in reverse sorted order)

algorithms.stability: Stable (Equal elements are never swapped across each other)

viva_questions.question: How can bubble sort be optimized for an already-sorted array?
viva_questions.answer: By using a boolean flag 'swapped'. If an entire inner pass completes without a single swap, the array is sorted and the algorithm breaks immediately, running in O(n) time.

viva_questions.question: Is bubble sort stable?
viva_questions.answer: Yes, because adjacent elements are only swapped when arr[j] > arr[j+1], preserving the relative order of duplicate values.

algorithms.name: Merge Sort
algorithms.definition: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that recursively halves the array until individual elements are reached, and then merges the sorted halves into a completely sorted array.
algorithms.working_principle: 1. Divide: Split the array into two halves at mid = l + (r - l) / 2. 2. Conquer: Recursively call mergeSort on left half and right half. 3. Combine: Call merge() to combine the two sorted halves using an auxiliary buffer.

time_complexity.worst: O(n log n) (Guaranteed across all input arrangements)

algorithms.space_complexity: O(n) auxiliary memory for buffer arrays during merge step
algorithms.stability: Stable (L[i] <= R[j] keeps duplicate elements in original order)
algorithms.in_place: No (Out-of-place due to O(n) temp array)

viva_questions.question: What is the recurrence relation for merge sort?
viva_questions.answer: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Solving with Master Theorem Case 2 yields T(n) = O(n log n).

viva_questions.question: Why is merge sort preferred for sorting linked lists?
viva_questions.answer: Because linked lists can be merged in O(1) extra space simply by updating pointers, overcoming the O(n) memory penalty on arrays.

algorithms.name: Quick Sort
algorithms.definition: Quick Sort is a divide-and-conquer in-place sorting algorithm that partitions an array around a chosen pivot element such that all smaller elements are placed before the pivot and all larger elements after it.
algorithms.working_principle: 1. Pick a pivot (commonly last element). 2. Partition: rearrange array so elements <= pivot are to left, and > pivot to right. Place pivot at its final correct index. 3. Recursively call quickSort on left and right partitions.
dry_run: Place pivot: swap(arr[i+1], arr[high]) -> swap arr[4] (80) with arr[6] (70) -> [10, 30, 40, 50, 70, 90, 80]
Pivot 70 is placed at index 4. Recurse on left [10,30,40,50] and right [90,80].

time_complexity.best: O(n log n) (Pivot always divides array into two balanced halves)
time_complexity.worst: O(n^2) (When pivot is consistently smallest or largest, e.g., already sorted array with end pivot)

algorithms.space_complexity: O(log n) auxiliary stack space for recursion (O(n) in worst case)
algorithms.stability: Unstable (Swapping elements around pivot disrupts order of duplicates)

viva_questions.question: How can the worst-case O(n^2) of Quick Sort be avoided?
viva_questions.answer: By using Randomized Pivot selection (picking pivot at a random index) or Median-of-Three pivot selection (median of first, middle, last elements).

viva_questions.question: Why is Quick Sort usually faster in practice than Merge Sort?
viva_questions.answer: Quick Sort is in-place and exhibits excellent cache locality (spatial locality), with lower constant factors in its inner loop compared to Merge Sort's array copying.

algorithms.name: Insertion Sort
algorithms.definition: Insertion Sort is a simple in-place comparison sort that builds the final sorted array one item at a time by repeatedly taking the next element and inserting it into its correct position within the already sorted portion.
algorithms.working_principle: Analogous to sorting playing cards in hand: Start with the second element (index 1). Store it in `key`. Compare `key` with preceding elements. Shift all elements greater than `key` one position to the right. Insert `key` into the empty spot. Repeat for all elements.
dry_run: Pass 1 (i=1, key=11): Compare 11 with 12. 12 > 11 -> shift 12 right -> insert 11 at [0] -> [11, 12, 13, 5, 6]
Pass 2 (i=2, key=13): Compare 13 with 12. 12 < 13 -> no shift -> 13 stays at [2] -> [11, 12, 13, 5, 6]
Pass 3 (i=3, key=5):  Compare 5 with 13, 12, 11 -> shift all right -> insert 5 at [0] -> [5, 11, 12, 13, 6]
Pass 4 (i=4, key=6):  Compare 6 with 13, 12, 11 -> shift 13, 12, 11 right -> insert 6 at [1] -> [5, 6, 11, 12, 13]
Array fully sorted in n-1 = 4 passes.

time_complexity.best: O(n) (When array is already sorted; inner while loop condition fails on first check)
time_complexity.worst: O(n^2) (When array is in reverse sorted order; maximum shifts required)

algorithms.stability: Stable (Only shifts when arr[j] > key, never when equal)

viva_questions.question: Why is Insertion Sort preferred for nearly sorted or small datasets?
viva_questions.answer: It is adaptive: running in O(n) linear time when data is already nearly sorted, with minimal constant factors and zero auxiliary memory allocation.

viva_questions.question: Is Insertion Sort an online algorithm?
viva_questions.answer: Yes, it can sort a list as it receives it in real-time, because it processes elements one by one without needing to know the complete dataset upfront.
